info.text: Interactive check questions for Lesson 1.2: Data That Lasts: FAIR Principles and the Scholarly Edition Workflow.

name.text: 01 Question: Where We Stand After Lesson 1.1

questiontext.text: What question does Lesson 1.2 answer, after Lesson 1.1 covered the tools?

generalfeedback.text: Lesson 1.1 gave the tools; Lesson 1.2 gives the purpose — scholarship others can find, check, and reuse.

answer.text: Not which tools we use, but what we are making and why — a scholarly edition built to be findable, checkable, and reusable.

feedback.text: Correct. The tools exist to serve the scholarly values introduced today.

answer.text: How to install the software faster next time.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Installation was Wednesday's work; today is conceptual.

answer.text: Which Greek dialect the course manuscripts use.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The course does not require Greek; today's question is about method, not language.

answer.text: How to choose a text editor.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The editor choice (VS Code) was settled in Lesson 1.1.

name.text: 02 Question: Why Ancient Documents Are Hard

questiontext.text: Which difficulty of ancient documents does the dispersion of witnesses across many libraries explain?

generalfeedback.text: Each digital method answers a concrete difficulty of the manuscripts: uniqueness, difficulty of hands, dispersion, fragility.

answer.text: Why digital methods emphasize shared catalogs and online images instead of travel to every holding library.

feedback.text: Correct. Dispersed evidence demands findable records and accessible images.

answer.text: Why all manuscripts must be transcribed in modern languages.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Transcription records the original language; dispersion is about access, not translation.

answer.text: Why ancient scribes wrote without word spacing.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Scriptio continua is a scribal habit, unrelated to where manuscripts ended up.

answer.text: Why printed editions are always unreliable.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Print editions were a serious solution; dispersion explains why sharing mechanisms arose at all.

name.text: 03 Question: What a Print Edition Records

questiontext.text: According to the lesson, what is the structural limit of a printed critical edition?

generalfeedback.text: An edition is an argument from evidence; print forces the argument to conclude and the evidence to shrink to apparatus.

answer.text: It must bake the editor's conclusions into the text while compressing the evidence into a few apparatus lines.

feedback.text: Correct. Print publishes conclusions; the evidence that justified them is nearly unrecoverable from the page.

answer.text: It cannot be printed in multiple copies.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Printing is exactly what print editions do well.

answer.text: It cannot represent accents or special characters.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Print handled special characters; the limit is evidential, not typographic.

answer.text: It costs too much for libraries to purchase.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Cost is not the structural limit named in the lesson.

name.text: 04 Question: What a Digital Edition Adds

questiontext.text: What does a digital scholarly edition publish that a print edition cannot?

generalfeedback.text: The digital edition makes claims inspectable: a reader can walk from the reading back to the manuscript image.

answer.text: The evidence itself — every transcription, variant, and decision as structured data a reader can re-examine.

feedback.text: Correct. Gabler's digital scholarly edition is a library of linked machine-readable evidence, not just conclusions.

answer.text: A prettier page layout than print.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Presentation is not the difference; the publication of evidence is.

answer.text: Translations of the text into modern languages.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Print editions have translations; the difference is the data structure.

answer.text: Faster printing at lower cost.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The lesson is not about production economics.

questiontext.text: What do the letters of FAIR stand for?

generalfeedback.text: FAIR = Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable — the checklist that turns a personal project into infrastructure.

answer.text: Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable.

feedback.text: Correct. Wilkinson et al. 2016 stated these as the criteria for well-managed research data.

answer.text: Formal, Archived, Indexed, Refined.

feedback.text: Incorrect. These are related data-management ideas but not the FAIR letters.

answer.text: Fast, Accurate, Integrated, Reproducible.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Reproducibility is a goal FAIR supports, but not one of the four letters.

answer.text: Findable, Authenticated, Interlinked, Ratable.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Close on the first letter only; the rest are invented.

questiontext.text: What does the lesson's 'FAIR before the Internet' section argue?

generalfeedback.text: Catalogs made manuscripts findable, facsimiles accessible, and apparatus reusable — with paper.

answer.text: Library catalogs, facsimiles, and print editions already pursued findability, accessibility, and reuse for centuries.

feedback.text: Correct. The internet changed the scale and mechanism; the scholarly values predate it.

answer.text: Data management was invented by funding agencies in 2016.

feedback.text: Incorrect. 2016 is when FAIR was formalized, not when the values arose.

answer.text: Manuscript catalogs were useless before computers could search them.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Printed catalogs and indexes were genuinely used for discovery.

answer.text: Print editions failed every FAIR criterion completely.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The lesson argues print succeeded at F, A, and partially R — at smaller scale.

questiontext.text: What are the F-and-A layers for manuscripts today?

generalfeedback.text: Your own passage choice this week relies on exactly these layers: a catalog record plus accessible images.

answer.text: Shared catalogs (Pinakes, LDAB, Papyri.info) make them findable; IIIF image servers make them accessible.

feedback.text: Correct. Catalog records are the metadata layer; IIIF URLs are the retrieval layer.

answer.text: Microfilm archives and interlibrary loan.

feedback.text: Incorrect. These are the older mechanism the lesson says has been superseded.

answer.text: Social media posts by libraries.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Discovery runs on structured catalogs, not social feeds.

answer.text: Commercial ebook platforms.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Manuscript images are served through IIIF, not ebook stores.

questiontext.text: Why does the course insist on TEI tags rather than a private markup scheme?

generalfeedback.text: Interoperability means choosing TEI, Dublin Core, CTS URNs, and IIIF over private formats so projects compose.

answer.text: Shared vocabularies let data from different projects combine — that is the I in FAIR.

feedback.text: Correct. If every project invents its own tags, no tool or scholar can merge the results.

answer.text: TEI tags are shorter and easier to type.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI is often more verbose; the reason is shared meaning.

answer.text: TEI is required by the university's software licenses.

feedback.text: Incorrect. No such requirement exists; the reason is scholarly interoperability.

answer.text: Private schemes are illegal under copyright law.

feedback.text: Incorrect. They are legal; they are simply isolating.

questiontext.text: Which three things deliver the R of FAIR for a dataset?

generalfeedback.text: Git history, TEI headers, and reconciliation reports are where documentation, license, and provenance live.

answer.text: Documentation, an open license, and provenance.

feedback.text: Correct. Documentation explains the data, the license permits reuse, provenance records where each piece came from.

answer.text: A beautiful website, a logo, and social media accounts.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Presentation is not reusability; a stranger must be able to understand and legally reuse the data.

answer.text: Encryption, backups, and compression.

feedback.text: Incorrect. These are preservation practices, not the FAIR-R requirements named.

answer.text: Peer review, print publication, and indexing.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Those help findability, but R is about documentation, license, and provenance.

questiontext.text: What is the correct order of the standard edition workflow's first three stages?

generalfeedback.text: Cataloguing → images → transcription → reconciliation/normalization → collation → linguistic markup → translation/annotation → presentation.

answer.text: Cataloguing the witnesses, then getting images, then transcription.

feedback.text: Correct. You must know what witnesses exist, look at them, and only then read them into plain text.

answer.text: Transcription, then cataloguing, then publication.

feedback.text: Incorrect. You cannot transcribe before you know what to look at.

answer.text: Publication, translation, then collation.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That runs the pipeline backwards; presentation is the last stage.

answer.text: Linguistic markup, images, then cataloguing.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Linguistic analysis comes late in the workflow, after the text is established.

questiontext.text: What does cataloguing a manuscript witness involve, and why does it come first?

generalfeedback.text: Week 2 has you write your passage's catalog record as a TEI header — the first scholarly act of your project.

answer.text: Recording its identifier, shelfmark, date, and contents in metadata — it fixes the scope of the evidence.

feedback.text: Correct. A mistake here (a missed witness) propagates into every later stage of the edition.

answer.text: Photographing the manuscript at high resolution.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That is the images stage; cataloguing is metadata, not photography.

answer.text: Transcribing the text letter by letter.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Transcription is stage 3; cataloguing precedes it.

answer.text: Publishing the finished edition online.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That is the presentation stage at the very end.

questiontext.text: What does IIIF provide for manuscript images?

generalfeedback.text: Record the IIIF address of your passage's images — provenance and findability in one act.

answer.text: Standard web addresses for images and regions of images, so any viewer can display and annotate any library's images.

feedback.text: Correct. IIIF is the interoperability layer for digitized manuscript images.

answer.text: Automatic transcription of the images into text.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That is HTR (Transkribus), a different workflow stage.

answer.text: Color printing of facsimile volumes.

feedback.text: Incorrect. IIIF is a web-image framework, not a print technology.

answer.text: Translation of the image's text.

feedback.text: Incorrect. IIIF moves pixels, not meanings.

questiontext.text: What is the difference between a diplomatic and a normalized transcription?

generalfeedback.text: The transcription is where the manuscript first becomes computable — and HTR accelerates but never replaces verification.

answer.text: A diplomatic transcription records exactly what the scribe wrote; a normalized one regularizes spelling and layout by decision.

feedback.text: Correct. Week 4 will have you practice both and feel the trade-off.

answer.text: Diplomatic means handwritten; normalized means typed.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Both are typed in this course; the difference is fidelity to the source.

answer.text: Diplomatic is done by diplomats; normalized by scholars.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The terms describe transcription styles, not who performs them.

answer.text: Normalized transcriptions keep all the scribe's errors.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That is the diplomatic style; normalization regularizes by recorded decision.

questiontext.text: What does a reconciliation report contribute to an edition?

generalfeedback.text: Week 5 measures character and word error rates of the HTR and AI passes against your Tuesday ground truth.

answer.text: Measured error rates for each transcription source against hand-made ground truth.

feedback.text: Correct. Measured quality — not impressions — is what makes the text trustworthy and reusable.

answer.text: A list of libraries that own the manuscript.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That belongs to cataloguing, the first stage.

answer.text: The final published translation.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Translation is stage 7; reconciliation is about checking transcriptions.

answer.text: A log of Git commit messages.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Commits help, but the reconciliation report is specifically about error rates.

questiontext.text: What does collation produce in a critical edition?

generalfeedback.text: Because transcriptions are plain text in a repository, the collation is repeatable in seconds whenever a transcript improves.

answer.text: The apparatus — the systematic record of where witnesses' texts differ.

feedback.text: Correct. Tools like CollateX align transcriptions and output variant positions as data.

answer.text: A photograph of every page.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Images are stage 2; collation compares already-transcribed texts.

answer.text: A dictionary of the ancient language.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Lexicography is a separate enterprise from collation.

answer.text: The library's catalog record.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That is cataloguing, stage 1.

questiontext.text: What does lemmatization add to a transcribed text?

generalfeedback.text: Morphological tagging, lemmatization, and syntax tagging turn a readable text into a queryable dataset.

answer.text: Links between each word form and its dictionary headword, so all forms of one word can be found together.

feedback.text: Correct. CLTK provides first-pass lemmatizers; human verification keeps the tagsets honest.

answer.text: Audio recordings of the text being read aloud.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Lemmatization is a textual analysis layer, not audio.

answer.text: Page images embedded in the file.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Images belong to stage 2.

answer.text: A list of libraries holding the manuscript.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That is cataloguing metadata, not linguistic markup.

questiontext.text: Why do digital editions keep the annotation layer separate from the text layer?

generalfeedback.text: Aligned translations (Alpheios) and structured annotations (Recogito, CATMA) are reusable data layers.

answer.text: Because the text is evidence and the annotations are arguments — keeping them separable lets future readers accept, reject, or extend each independently.

feedback.text: Correct. Separability is FAIR thinking applied to interpretation.

answer.text: To save space on the web server.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The separation is scholarly, not a storage economy.

answer.text: Because annotations are secret.

feedback.text: Incorrect. They are published; they are just structured and separable.

answer.text: Because translations are illegal without separation.

feedback.text: Incorrect. No law requires it; the principle is evidential hygiene.

questiontext.text: What principle lets one TEI file render as a website, a print PDF, and a machine interface?

generalfeedback.text: Presentation is where the FAIR audit happens: findable, accessible, interoperable, reusable — or it is a poster, not an edition.

answer.text: Separation of data from presentation.

feedback.text: Correct. The same data can feed many renderings — that is what makes the edition FAIR-auditable at publication.

answer.text: Compressing the XML into a smaller format.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Compression is irrelevant; the principle is about structure, not size.

answer.text: Translating the text into English first.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Rendering is not translation.

answer.text: Locking the file with a password.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That would defeat accessibility, the A of FAIR.

name.text: 19 Question: The Workflow Is the Semester

questiontext.text: How do RELS 398's modules relate to the standard edition workflow?

generalfeedback.text: Cataloguing (2) → images (3) → transcription (4) → reconciliation (5) → normalization (6) → collation (7–8) → lemmatization (9) → consolidation/alignment (10–11) → commentary (12) → publication (13).

answer.text: Modules 2–13 walk the workflow stages in order, each practiced manual → deterministic → AI-assisted.

feedback.text: Correct. The workflow supplies the 'what'; the three-step cycle supplies the 'how'.

answer.text: The modules follow the history of computing from the 1950s to today.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The order comes from the edition workflow, not computing history.

answer.text: Modules are unordered electives you may take in any sequence.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The sequence mirrors the workflow because each stage feeds the next.

answer.text: Only the final module relates to editions at all.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Every module is one stage of the edition workflow.

name.text: 20 Question: Editing and Validating XML in VS Code

questiontext.text: How does VS Code support professional-grade TEI XML editing and validation in this course?

generalfeedback.text: Week 2: hand-write a TEI header Tuesday, then validate it in VS Code on Wednesday — the errors teach you what a schema is.

answer.text: Through an XML extension that provides real-time schema validation (RELAX NG, W3C Schema, DTD), tag autocomplete, and diagnostics as you type.

feedback.text: Correct. Validation catches structural and syntax errors at typing time instead of discovery at publication time.

answer.text: It converts XML documents into Word format automatically.

feedback.text: Incorrect. VS Code is designed for plain text and structured markup, not proprietary Word files.

answer.text: It automatically translates ancient Greek without human intervention.

feedback.text: Incorrect. No text editor translates; translation requires philological analysis and dedicated tools.

answer.text: It requires a costly proprietary enterprise license to enable XML editing.

feedback.text: Incorrect. VS Code and its XML extensions are completely free, open, and cross-platform.

name.text: 21 Question: VS Code as the Unified Scholarly Workbench

questiontext.text: Why does this course use VS Code as a unified editing environment for both plain text and XML?

generalfeedback.text: Establish now: one repository, commit at checkpoints, plain text always.

answer.text: It eliminates tool fragmentation by unifying plain text notes, XML validation, Git version control, and Python in one free, portable application.

feedback.text: Correct. A unified workbench keeps scholarly attention focused on the methods and texts rather than switching between disparate proprietary editors.

answer.text: VS Code is strictly for beginners and cannot handle real XML markup.

feedback.text: Incorrect. With language server extensions, VS Code handles industrial-scale XML and software engineering.

answer.text: Using VS Code eliminates the need for Git version control entirely.

feedback.text: Incorrect. VS Code integrates with Git directly; Git remains essential for version control and the audit trail.

answer.text: Because XML can only be edited inside a web browser.

feedback.text: Incorrect. XML files are plain text files that can be authored and validated in any standard desktop text editor.

questiontext.text: Which accounts does the course require this week, and what does each serve?

generalfeedback.text: Prefer platforms that export your data in open formats — platforms you can leave.

answer.text: GitHub (repo hosting), Transkribus (HTR in Module 4), and Zotero (bibliography) — plus the THREAD documentation.

feedback.text: Correct. Each platform maps to a workflow stage you will use this term.

answer.text: Instagram, TikTok, and Discord.

feedback.text: Incorrect. None of these is part of the scholarly workflow.

answer.text: Only GitHub; nothing else is needed all term.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Transkribus and Zotero are needed for Modules 4–5 and your bibliography.

answer.text: A paid commercial editor subscription, MATLAB, and SPSS.

feedback.text: Incorrect. We use free, open tooling (VS Code, Git), and MATLAB/SPSS are not part of this workflow.

name.text: 23 Question: Platforms Must Be FAIR Too

questiontext.text: What does it mean to evaluate a platform as a 'data custody decision'?

generalfeedback.text: Zotero exports open formats; GitHub repos clone completely; that is why they are in the toolkit.

answer.text: Asking where your data lives, in what format, how it can be exported, and under whose control it stands.

feedback.text: Correct. A tool with a real export path composes with the FAIR stack; one without becomes a lock on your research.

answer.text: Choosing whichever platform is cheapest.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Cost matters, but custody is about data control, not price.

answer.text: Uploading nothing to any online service ever.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The course uses online services throughout; the point is choosing them wisely.

answer.text: Requiring all collaborators to use the same password manager.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Password practice is separate from data custody.

questiontext.text: Why do standard OCR systems fail on printed critical editions?

generalfeedback.text: The study is the whole workflow in miniature: findable inputs, machine transcription, human ground truth, structured open output.

answer.text: Editions are dense two-dimensional layouts — text interleaved with apparatus, brackets, and abbreviations — which plain OCR destroys.

feedback.text: Correct. The 2026 Angleraud et al. study trains models to recognize layout roles, not just characters.

answer.text: Editions are always handwritten in cursive.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Printed editions are typeset; the failure is structural, not a handwriting problem.

answer.text: Greek letters are too colorful for scanners.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Color is irrelevant; structure is the issue.

answer.text: OCR is illegal to use on published editions.

feedback.text: Incorrect. There is no such law; the difficulty is technical.

name.text: 25 Question: Machine Learning and Philological Judgment

questiontext.text: What is the recurring lesson about AI in the edition workflow?

generalfeedback.text: Automation moves your effort from mechanical transcription toward judgment, verification, and designing checks.

answer.text: AI output is only trustworthy when measured against your own manual ground truth — the comparison is the scholarship.

feedback.text: Correct. Tuesday's manual work is the baseline that makes Friday's AI pass evaluable.

answer.text: AI should be trusted wherever it is faster than humans.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Speed without verification is how fluent nonsense enters scholarship.

answer.text: AI cannot do anything useful for ancient texts.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It does useful drafts; the point is they must be evaluated.

answer.text: Deterministic scripts are obsolete now that AI exists.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Wednesday's scripts are perfectly repeatable, which makes them auditable — a different virtue.

questiontext.text: Which set of criteria should guide your manuscript-passage choice?

generalfeedback.text: You are choosing the raw material for thirteen weeks — choose with the workflow in mind.

answer.text: 10–20 continuous lines, a good public image, manageable difficulty, a language you will work in, and sustained interest.

feedback.text: Correct. Enough substance to matter, few enough lines to double-key and translate.

answer.text: The longest continuous text you can find, to impress the instructor.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Oversized passages strand students by mid-semester.

answer.text: Whatever passage appears first in the textbook.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The criteria are about images, difficulty, and your sustained interest.

answer.text: A passage with no abbreviations or corrections whatsoever.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Some features make the work interesting; total simplicity removes the scholarship.

questiontext.text: Which check belongs in the five-point verification of a candidate passage?

generalfeedback.text: Image legible, identity established, text identified, self-contained boundaries, difficulty named.

answer.text: Confirm the manuscript has a catalog record and that a legible public image of the passage exists.

feedback.text: Correct. Image and identity are checks 1–2; boundaries, text identification, and named difficulty complete the five.

answer.text: Check that the passage has never been edited by anyone.

feedback.text: Incorrect. A prior edition is a help, not a disqualifier.

answer.text: Check that the library will mail the original manuscript to you.

feedback.text: Incorrect. You work from images; libraries do not lend codices by post.

answer.text: Check that the text is written in Latin alphabet only.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Greek and other ancient languages are welcome; the tools support them.

questiontext.text: What must be in your README.md and commit message by Friday's deadline?

generalfeedback.text: Committing the README is your first FAIR act: findable, documented, timestamped, attributed.

answer.text: Shelfmark and catalog ID, folio and line numbers, the text it contains, the image URL, expected difficulty — committed with a specific message.

feedback.text: Correct. This small file is the seed of your Week 2 TEI header and your project's provenance record.

answer.text: A full transcription of the passage with apparatus.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That is Weeks 4–8's work; today needs identity, location, image, and difficulty.

answer.text: A screenshot of the manuscript pasted into the README.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Record the image's URL; the README is plain text.

answer.text: Nothing — the choice only needs to be announced in class.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The deliverable is a committed file, not an announcement.

questiontext.text: Which items are on this week's setup checklist?

generalfeedback.text: Software, accounts, passage, commit, push, readings, lab access — all unblocking work.

answer.text: VS Code and Git configured, GitHub/Transkribus/Zotero accounts, passage chosen and committed, readings skimmed, lab login tested.

feedback.text: Correct. Setup debt cleared now keeps Week 2 about scholarship instead of configuration.

answer.text: Buying a tablet and stylus for note-taking.

feedback.text: Incorrect. No hardware purchase is on the list; the lab machines have the specialist software.

answer.text: memorizing the complete TEI tag vocabulary.

feedback.text: Incorrect. You will learn tags module by module; the checklist is about setup, not memorization.

answer.text: Translating the whole passage before Week 2.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Translation is Module 12; early translation is not on the checklist.

questiontext.text: How do FAIR, the workflow, and your passage fit together?

generalfeedback.text: Your README commit today and your published portfolio in December are the same act at two scales.

answer.text: FAIR gives the values, the eight-stage workflow the practice, and your passage the object all term.

feedback.text: Correct. Each stage's output feeds the next because the principles make the work cumulative and reusable.

answer.text: They are three separate assignments with no connection.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The connection is the deep fact: FAIR is what makes the workflow cumulative.

answer.text: FAIR replaces the need for a workflow.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Principles without a pipeline do not produce editions.

answer.text: The passage is only relevant to the final module.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Every module from 2 to 13 operates on your passage.
